headline: Europe grows tougher on trade with China

sources.title: EU sends envoy to Beijing as rising exports from China raise economic anxiety (Associated Press)
In Beijing, EU trade envoy says deficit with China 'unsustainable' (AFP, via 24 News HD)
EU-China trade talks begin in Beijing amid escalating pressure (Al Jazeera)
EU trade envoy eyes yawning goods deficit on first day of China visit (video, France 24)

chunks.text: On October 8, 2026, the European Union's trade chief {{sat down with}} China's [[commerce minister]] in Beijing for two days of talks. Europe's [[trade deficit]] with China is about 360 billion euros, or 410 billion dollars. The deficit keeps {{piling up}} by more than 1 billion dollars a day. The trade chief wants to {{bring down}} that number. Earlier in 2026, he gave Beijing an October [[deadline]] to show real results.

verbs.correct: To meet someone for serious talks
verbs.wrong: To send someone a list of demands
verbs.why: The boss sat down with the workers to discuss their pay. We need to sit down with the landlord about the repairs. The EU's trade chief sat down with China's commerce minister in Beijing on October 8, 2026.

verbs.correct: To grow bigger little by little
verbs.wrong: To be repaid in small amounts
verbs.why: Unpaid bills piled up while he was sick. Her debts began piling up after she lost her job. The EU's trade deficit with China keeps piling up by more than 1 billion dollars a day.
The store brought down its prices for the sale. Exercise can help bring down your blood pressure. The trade chief wants to bring down the EU's trade deficit with China.

chunks.text: Chinese exports to the European Union rose 15.3 percent in the first eight months of 2026. European leaders say [[state subsidies]] help Chinese companies sell steel, batteries and [[solar panels]] cheaply. Chinese [[carmakers]] are {{taking on}} Europe's [[best-known]] brands. Many fear that European workers will {{lose out}}. The head of the European Commission calls this another "China shock." In the United States in the early 2000s, Chinese competition helped {{wipe out}} hundreds of thousands of [[factory jobs]].

verbs.correct: To try to beat a rival
verbs.wrong: To buy a share of a company
verbs.why: Our small team will take on the champions on Saturday. The new coffee shop is taking on the big chains. Chinese carmakers are taking on Europe's best-known brands.

verbs.correct: To be hurt by a change
verbs.why: Local shops lost out when the big mall opened. Taxi drivers lost out when ride apps became popular. Leaders worry that European workers will lose out to cheap Chinese competition.

verbs.wrong: To count something a second time
verbs.why: The storm wiped out the town's corn crop. One bad year wiped out all of their savings. Competition from China helped wipe out hundreds of thousands of factory jobs in the United States.

chunks.text: On October 7, the European Parliament voted 454 to 86 for a [[resolution]] calling for a tougher China [[policy]]. In a letter, the leaders of France and Germany {{stepped up}} the pressure. They want a tool to {{push back}} quickly against countries that [[harm]] Europe's economy. But not every EU country will {{go along with}} [[tough measures]]. Spain has been friendlier toward China. Its prime minister has visited Beijing four times in three years.

verbs.why: Police stepped up patrols after the robberies. The school stepped up its safety checks this year. The leaders of France and Germany stepped up the pressure with a letter.

verbs.wrong: To pay a fine to another country
verbs.why: Parents pushed back against the plan to close the school. Workers are pushing back against longer hours. France and Germany want a tool that lets the EU push back quickly against countries that harm its economy.

verbs.correct: To accept and support a plan
verbs.why: I didn't like the idea, but I went along with it. Most of the class went along with the teacher's plan. Not every EU country will go along with tough measures against China.

chunks.text: China's commerce ministry warned France and Germany against [[protectionist]] steps. It said such steps would hurt others and help no one. Days before the talks, China opened a [[trade investigation]] into a European chemical. Europe asked China to {{cut back on}} its exports of [[hybrid cars]], but Beijing opposes such limits. The talks are meant to {{head off}} a [[trade war]]. Experts doubt the two sides will {{work out}} a [[broad deal]] in these talks.

verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.wrong: To elect the leader of something
verbs.why: I'm trying to cut back on sugar. The factory cut back on night shifts this year. Europe asked China to cut back on its exports of hybrid cars.

verbs.correct: To stop something before it starts
verbs.why: The city fixed the dam to head off a flood. A quick apology can head off a fight. The talks in Beijing are meant to head off a trade war.

verbs.correct: To reach an agreement after talks
verbs.wrong: To write a report about talks
verbs.why: The two companies worked out a deal on prices. My brother and I worked out a plan to share the car. Experts doubt that the EU and China will work out a broad deal in Beijing.

mainIdea.s: Europe is getting tougher on trade because cheap Chinese goods threaten its factories and workers. Its trade chief held talks in Beijing as lawmakers and leaders asked for stronger tools.
mainIdea.why: The EU's trade chief sat down with China's commerce minister in Beijing. Lawmakers and leaders want a tougher policy because they fear European workers will lose out.

mainIdea.s: All countries in the European Union have agreed to place new taxes on Chinese products. The EU sent its trade chief to Beijing to announce these new limits to China's commerce minister in person.
mainIdea.why: Close, but no new taxes were announced in Beijing. Not every EU country will go along with tough measures, and Spain has been friendlier toward China.

mainIdea.s: Several big European carmakers have opened new electric car plants in China this year. They hope to win more buyers there, since car sales across Europe have been weak for a long time now.
mainIdea.why: This story is about the EU's huge trade deficit with China. Europe wants to bring down that deficit and is pressing China in talks in Beijing.

lines.text: Did you see that the EU's trade chief {{sat down with}} China's commerce minister in Beijing?
I did. Is this about the trade deficit?
Yes. It keeps {{piling up}} by more than a billion dollars a day.
That's a lot of money. I can see why Europe wants to {{bring down}} that number.
European leaders also say Chinese state subsidies make the competition unfair. They want [[a level playing field]].
And Chinese carmakers are {{taking on}} the big European brands, right?
Right. Many people worry that factory workers will {{lose out}}.
Like the "China shock" in the United States, when so many factory jobs were {{wiped out}}.
Exactly. Now France and Germany have {{stepped up}} the pressure. They want a tool to {{push back}} fast.
But trade is [[a two-way street]]. Won't China respond?
It already has. It opened a trade investigation into a European chemical.
Are all the EU countries [[on the same page]]?
Not really. Spain may not {{go along with}} tough measures.
So both sides could [[play hardball]]. Can the talks {{head off}} a trade war?
Experts doubt they'll {{work out}} a broad deal this time. Smaller deals are possible.
Well, maybe they'll take it [[one step at a time]].

expressions.def: A fair situation where everyone has the same chance to win
ex: Small shops just want a level playing field with the big stores.

expressions.def: Used to say that both sides must do their part
ex: Respect is a two-way street.

expressions.def: Agreeing about what to do or how to do it
ex: Let's make sure we're all on the same page before the meeting.

expressions.def: To act in a very tough way to get what you want
ex: The landlord decided to play hardball over the rent.
Both teams played hardball during the contract talks.

expressions.def: Used to say that something will be done slowly, in small parts
ex: Learning a language happens one step at a time.
We're fixing the old house one step at a time.
